title: Three baskets
hook: discipline, discourses, and the higher teaching: the Pali canon

segments.voice: Yesterday: Theravada, and your line, still walking at dawn. Today, the scripture the elders kept.

In Mandalay, in Myanmar, a pagoda is surrounded by small white shrines, row after row, like a quiet city. Inside each one stands a marble slab, taller than a person, carved on both sides with tiny letters. Walk them all and you've walked through a book. A Burmese king had the whole scripture of his tradition carved in stone, slab after slab, so it would outlast palm leaves and paper. A book made of marble. What's carved there comes in three parts.
screen: `A CITY OF WHITE SHRINES.` → `MARBLE SLABS, BOTH SIDES CARVED.` → `A BOOK MADE OF MARBLE.`

segments.voice: Tipitaka. Ti, three. Piṭaka, basket. The three baskets. Nobody is completely sure why baskets. One old explanation pictures workers on a building site passing baskets of earth from hand to hand, the way the teaching passed from teacher to student by memory before it was written. The first basket is the Vinaya, the discipline: the rules for monks and nuns and, charmingly, the stories behind them, what happened that made the Buddha say, from now on, don't do that. The second is the Suttas, the discourses: the Buddha's talks and conversations, in five collections. The long ones, the middle-length ones, the connected ones grouped by topic, the numbered ones grouped by how many items they list, and a fifth collection of shorter works. That fifth one holds the Dhammapada, which this path has quoted before. One of its verses sums up the whole in Max Müller's English: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." The third basket is the Abhidhamma, the higher teaching: seven books that analyze the mind and experience into their tiniest moments, like a chemistry of consciousness. Theravada Buddhists study it seriously, and in Myanmar it's especially honored. Printed, the three baskets fill a long shelf. A British scholar, T. W. Rhys Davids, founded the Pali Text Society to publish and translate them, and his own translations are among those this path draws on.
screen: `TI: THREE. PIṬAKA: BASKET.` · `VINAYA: THE DISCIPLINE.` · `SUTTAS: THE DISCOURSES.` · `ABHIDHAMMA: THE HIGHER TEACHING.` · then, large: `THREE BASKETS.`

segments.voice: On one breath, name the first basket silently: discipline, how you live. On the next, discourses, what the Buddha taught; on the next, the higher teaching, how the mind works, moment by moment. Go around a few times, then let the names go and notice this moment of mind, the one the third basket tries to describe.
Tipitaka. The three baskets of the Pali canon: the discipline, the discourses, and the higher teaching.
Your line: a book made of marble. Three baskets, and one teaching inside. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada monks memorize and chant passages from the three baskets, recite the monastic rules every two weeks, and in Myanmar monks can sit formal exams on the canon.

fork.setup: you want to know why monks don't eat after noon. which basket do you open?
fork.reveal: the Vinaya holds the monastic rules and the stories of how each came about.

original.note: Pali tipiṭaka: three baskets; Sanskrit tripiṭaka.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Pali canon is one book, like a Bible.
what it means: three baskets: discipline, discourses and the higher teaching, a long shelf in print.

what a scholar hears: the Kuthodaw slabs in Mandalay were carved under King Mindon in the 1860s, and the canon was recited at the council he convened in 1871; the Pali Text Society, founded by Rhys Davids in 1881, still publishes the canon.

notes: Check Müller's exact wording of Dhammapada 183 in SBE 10 (quoted from memory, including the parenthetical '(all)').
Kuthodaw Pagoda: 729 slabs, carving completed 1868 under King Mindon; the 'Fifth Council' was 1871. Confirm dates.
The 'baskets passed hand to hand' explanation of piṭaka is one traditional/scholarly suggestion; presented as uncertain.
Pali Text Society founded 1881 by T. W. Rhys Davids: confirm.
